Key Concepts to Master

CONCEPT 1
Plant Pollination Methods
6 questions
Wind-pollinated flowers have protruding anthers and feathery stigmas. Animal-pollinated flowers use brightly-coloured petals and nectar to attract insects.
feathery stigma protruding
CONCEPT 2
Seed Dispersal Mechanisms
8 questions
Fruits use water, wind, animals, or splitting to scatter seeds. For example, fibrous husks trap air to float on water, while stiff hairs cling to animal fur.
fibrous husk stiff hair
CONCEPT 3
Importance of Dispersal
4 questions
Scattering seeds further away from the parent plant prevents overcrowding. This reduces competition for sunlight, space, water, and mineral salts.
competition overcrowding
CONCEPT 4
Plant Fertilisation
5 questions
After pollination, the male cell from a pollen grain fuses with the female cell inside the ovule. The ovary develops into a fruit and ovules become seeds.
fertilisation fuses
CONCEPT 5
Human Reproductive System
3 questions
The testes produce sperms (male reproductive cells) and the ovaries produce eggs (female reproductive cells). A block in the fallopian tubes prevents fertilisation.
testes sperms
CONCEPT 6
Seed Germination
2 questions
Seeds need warmth, oxygen, and water to germinate. The seed leaf provides stored food for the seedling until it grows green leaves to make its own food.
warmth, oxygen and water seed leaf

Why Open-Ended is Harder Than MCQ

In MCQs, you can simply recognize the correct dispersal method or reproductive part. In Open-Ended questions, you must accurately construct the causal chain using exact terminology, such as explaining how a fibrous husk traps air to allow floating, or distinguishing between pollination (transfer) and fertilisation (fusing).

Common P5 Open-Ended Writing Mistakes

Avoid these frequent pitfalls to secure full marks in exams.

Critical Distinctions for P5

Keywords to Write in Your P5 Answers

Linking Words

Use words like "further away from the parent plant", "to allow it to", and "prevents" to connect a physical trait to its survival advantage.

Wrong Written Answers — P5 Traps

Answer Formulas

EXPLAIN Phenomenon / Function

Use this to connect an observable trait (like hooks or fibrous husks) to its reproductive advantage.

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

The seeds have hooks / stiff hair to cling onto the fur of animals. The seeds are scattered when the animals move further away from parent.
What to AVOID:
Stating the method without explaining the mechanism (e.g., "It uses animal dispersal" instead of "Hooks cling onto animal fur").
Forgetting to mention the final result: "dropped further away from the parent plant".

DESCRIBE Process / Sequence

Use this to outline the steps of a biological process like fertilisation or fleshy fruit dispersal.

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

The seeds are dispersed by animals the animal will be attracted by the brightly-coloured fruit and the animals will eat the sweet and juicy fruit and will spit out the seeds when eating the fruit.
What to AVOID:
Skipping the middle action (e.g., saying the animal eats it and the seed grows, without mentioning it is spat out or passed in droppings).

COMPARE Two Concepts

Use this to contrast the properties of two items, such as dispersal methods.

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

Seeds dispersed by splitting would be dispersed nearer to the parent plant as compared to wind.
What to AVOID:
Only describing one side of the comparison.
Failing to use comparative words like "nearer", "longer", or "more easily".

SUGGEST Action / Improvement

Use this when modifying an experiment to test a specific variable.

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

(i) Change the petal (coloured) cards to different sizes. (ii) Keep the number of drops of sweet-smelling substance the same.
What to AVOID:
Suggesting changes that alter multiple variables at once, breaking a fair test.

STATE Direct Answer

Use this for 1-mark recall or direct data relationship questions.

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

As the duration of soaking increases, the number of seeds germinated increases.
What to AVOID:
Writing long paragraphs when only a single fact or relationship statement is required.

GIVE_REASON Explain an Outcome

Use this to justify why a specific consequence happened, often using negative logic (what prevented it).

Real Example from a P5 Model Answer:

No. As the sperm is not able to enter R or S, the fallopian tube. Thus, the sperm cannot fuse with the egg and fertilisation cannot take place.
What to AVOID:
Stating the outcome ("no baby") without the anatomical mechanism ("sperm cannot fuse with the egg").

Universal Open-Ended Answer Checklist

✓ Did I use exact science keywords (e.g., "fertilisation" instead of "joins")?
✓ Did I specify the exact plant/animal part involved (e.g., stigma, ovule, fallopian tube)?
✓ For dispersal questions, did I mention "prevents overcrowding and competition"?
✓ For experiments, did I explicitly state the relationship ("As X increases, Y increases")?
✓ Did I answer the specific question asked (Yes/No) before explaining?
✓ Did I trace the cause to the final effect (trait → action → advantage)?
